title: California advance warning sign spacing by speed (CA MUTCD Table 6B-1)
topic: Traffic control: advance warning signs
text: California's Table 6B-1 in the CA MUTCD 2026 sets advance warning sign spacing by speed on urban streets, which the national table does not. Distances A, B and C are the same within each row. Urban, 25 mph or less: 100 ft. 30 mph: 150 ft. 35 mph: 200 ft. 40 mph: 250 ft. 45 mph: 300 ft. Urban, 50 mph or more: 350 ft. Rural: 500 ft. Expressway or freeway: A 1,000 ft, B 1,500 ft, C 2,640 ft. A is from the taper or point of restriction to the first sign, B from the first to the second sign, C from the second to the third. Use the posted speed limit, the off-peak 85th-percentile speed before work starts, or the expected operating speed. So three signs on a 35 mph city street sit 200 ft apart, 600 ft in all. These are recommended minimums; the encroachment permit or the approved traffic control plan can ask for more, and on State highways the Caltrans Standard Plans govern.
source: CA MUTCD 2026 (Caltrans, eff. Jan. 18, 2026), Table 6B-1 and footnotes; Section 6B.04

title: California taper lengths by speed for a 12 ft lane (CA MUTCD Table 6B-3(CA))
topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
text: California's CA MUTCD 2026 prints the taper lengths for a 12 ft offset in Table 6B-3(CA). Merging taper L, then shifting taper L/2, then shoulder taper L/3, in feet. 20 mph: 80, 40, 27. 25 mph: 125, 63, 42. 30 mph: 180, 90, 60. 35 mph: 245, 123, 82. 40 mph: 320, 160, 107. 45 mph: 540, 270, 180. 50 mph: 600, 300, 200. 55 mph: 660, 330, 220. 60 mph: 720, 360, 240. 65 mph: 780, 390, 260. 70 mph: 840, 420, 280. 75 mph: 900, 450, 300. Downstream taper: 50 ft, 100 ft maximum. For another width use the formula: W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less, W x S at 45 mph or more. S is the posted speed limit, the off-peak 85th-percentile speed before work starts, or the expected operating speed. Devices in the downstream taper and in the one-lane two-way taper go about 20 ft apart. On State highways use the Caltrans Standard Plans for traffic control systems, T9 to T27 (Section 6B.08).
source: CA MUTCD 2026, Section 6B.08 paras. 4, 8, 12, 14, 16; Tables 6B-3, 6B-3(CA), 6B-4

title: California buffer space and flagger distance, including downgrades (Table 6B-2(CA))
topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
text: California's CA MUTCD 2026 uses the national stopping sight distance table for a longitudinal buffer space or a flagger station on a level road, and adds Table 6B-2(CA) for downgrades. Level road (Table 6B-2): 25 mph 155 ft, 30 mph 200 ft, 35 mph 250 ft, 40 mph 305 ft, 45 mph 360 ft, 50 mph 425 ft, 55 mph 495 ft, 60 mph 570 ft, 65 mph 645 ft. Downgrades, as minus 3 percent, minus 6 percent, minus 9 percent: 25 mph 158, 165, 173 ft. 30 mph 205, 215, 227 ft. 35 mph 257, 271, 287 ft. 40 mph 315, 333, 354 ft. 45 mph 378, 400, 427 ft. 50 mph 446, 474, 507 ft. 55 mph 520, 553, 593 ft. 60 mph 598, 638, 686 ft. 65 mph 682, 728, 785 ft. Using the table for a buffer is an Option in Section 6B.06; no work, equipment, vehicles or material should be in the buffer. Flagger stations may be placed with the same distances and shall be lit at night except in emergencies (Section 6D.06).
source: CA MUTCD 2026, Section 6B.06 para. 11; Tables 6B-2 and 6B-2(CA); Section 6D.06 paras. 3, 5

title: California flagger training rule and paddle (CA MUTCD 6D.01, 8 CCR 1599)
topic: Traffic control: flaggers
text: California does not issue a state flagger card, but training is mandatory. The CA MUTCD 2026 adds a California Standard to Section 6D.01: flaggers shall be trained in the proper fundamentals of flagging moving traffic before being assigned as flaggers. The training covers nine topics, among them flagger equipment, the layout of the work zone, signaling to stop, proceed and slow, one-way traffic control, emergency vehicles, handling emergencies, hostile drivers, and flagging alone. The trainer shall have the qualifications and experience to teach it, and the employer shall keep the training records required by its Injury and Illness Prevention Program (8 CCR 3203). The Cal/OSHA rule is Construction Safety Orders section 1599. Paddle: a 24 by 24 inch STOP/SLOW paddle may be used where more emphasis is needed and speeds are 30 mph or more; on a staff, the bottom of the paddle should be at least 6 ft above the pavement. Flags are for emergencies, at least 24 inches square. Apparel is ANSI/ISEA 107-2015 Class 2 or 3, Class 3 recommended for flaggers at night (Section 6C.05). Flagger stations shall be lit at night except in emergencies.
source: CA MUTCD 2026, Sections 6D.01 paras. 2-5, 6D.02 paras. 4, 5a, 6D.03, 6D.06 para. 5, 6C.05; 8 CCR 1599, 3203

title: California work zone fines and construction speed zones (CVC 42009, 22362)
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: California Vehicle Code 42009 raises the penalty for listed moving violations in a highway construction or maintenance area: a misdemeanor fine is doubled, and an infraction is charged one category higher on the uniform traffic penalty schedule. It applies only when workers are actually doing the work and traffic control devices or warning signs tell drivers the workers are there. The listed offenses include speeding, obeying traffic devices, passing, right-of-way, turning, reckless driving and DUI. Speed zones: the CA MUTCD 2026 (Section 6B.01) says a reduced construction speed limit under Vehicle Code 22362 has to be documented in writing, cannot be set below 25 mph, is posted only where the work affects traffic, and the signs are covered or removed in non-working hours unless the condition is still there. Vehicle Code 21367 lets the agency doing the work regulate traffic through it. The contractor cannot post a regulatory speed limit on its own; the agency orders it.
source: Cal. Veh. Code 42009(a)-(c); Veh. Code 22362, 21367; CA MUTCD 2026 Section 6B.01 paras. 19a, 20c-20p
edition: Cal. Veh. Code 42009 as read 2026-11-20; CA MUTCD 2026
note: Vehicle Code text read on a third-party mirror (california.public.law); confirm on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.

title: California Caltrans standard plans for traffic control (T-series)
topic: Traffic control: typical setups for utility work
text: California State highway work uses the Caltrans Standard Plans for traffic control systems, which the CA MUTCD 2026 points to as T9 through T27 (Section 6B.08). From the 2026 Standard Plans digest: T9 carries the advance warning sign spacing table; T10 is the lane closure plan and T10A the complete closure and lane closure with partial shoulder use; T11 is a typical lane closure and T11A a changeable lane closure; T12 is a half-road closure; T13 covers reversible (one-lane, two-way) traffic control with flaggers, with T13B for residential driveways and low-volume side roads; T14 covers ramps; T15 and T16 are moving lane closures on multilane highways. A Caltrans encroachment permit will name the T-plan to use. City and county streets follow the CA MUTCD and the city's own permit conditions; many cities accept a T-plan or a typical application as the traffic control plan for a short utility job. Sheet titles for T13, T13A, T13C and T17 were not confirmed from the digest.
source: CA MUTCD 2026 Section 6B.08 para. 16; Caltrans 2026 Standard Plans digest (T9-T17)

title: Arizona work zone double fines (A.R.S. 28-710) and the signs
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: Arizona doubles the cost of speeding in a state highway work zone when workers are present. A.R.S. 28-710: in a state highway work zone marked by traffic control devices that show where it begins and ends, a driver may not exceed the speed shown on the devices; if workers are present, the driver pays the normal civil penalty plus an additional assessment equal to it. Half of the extra goes to the state highway work zone safety fund and half to the state highway fund. Signs: the Arizona Supplement to the MUTCD (Section 6G.08) says double fine signs in state highway work zones go up only when workers are present and come down or are covered when they are not, existing speed limit signs inside the double fine area are covered, and the layout should follow the ADOT Temporary Traffic Control Design Guidelines. Leaving the double fine signs up with no crew there is not allowed under that section. City streets are not state highway work zones under this statute.
source: A.R.S. 28-710(A)-(D); A.R.S. 28-652; ADOT Arizona Supplement to the MUTCD 11th Edition (Jan. 2026) Section 6G.08

title: Nevada double penalties in work zones (NRS 484B.130)
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: Nevada adds a second penalty, equal to the first, for speeding and other listed traffic offenses in a temporary traffic control zone (NRS 484B.130). It applies when construction, maintenance or repair workers are present, or when the road condition, such as narrowed or shifted lanes or an uneven surface, makes the violation more dangerous. The added penalty is capped at $1,000, 6 months in jail or 120 hours of community service. Signs are part of it: the agency or its contractor must put up a sign before the zone reading DOUBLE PENALTIES IN WORK ZONES, a sign at the beginning of the zone and a sign at the end. If the signs are missing the double penalty generally does not apply, unless the violation injured a worker or did $1,000 or more in property damage. Signs are not required for emergency zones or on roads posted 25 mph or less next to residential areas, and there the double penalty applies only with a worker injury or $1,000 or more in damage. So on a Nevada job, the three signs are the contractor's to set.
note: Read on nevada.public.law (mirror, accessed text dated May 2025); confirm on leg.state.nv.us.

title: Texas work zone fines double when workers are present (Transp. Code 472.022)
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: Texas Transportation Code 472.022 makes it an offense to disobey a warning sign or drive around a barricade, with a fine of $1 to $200. If it happens in a construction or maintenance work zone while workers are present, and the citation says so, the fine is $2 to $400. A stretch of road only counts as a construction or maintenance work zone for this purpose if it is marked by signs that say it is a work zone, show where the zone begins and ends, and state: Fines double when workers present. Mobile operations, as the Texas MUTCD defines them, are not included. Driving around a barricade placed because water is over the road is a Class B misdemeanor. For a crew this means the begin, end and fines-double signs have to be in the setup for the higher fines to apply.
source: Tex. Transp. Code 472.022
edition: Tex. Transp. Code 472.022, current as of Jan. 1, 2026
note: Read on FindLaw (current as of 2026-01-01); confirm on statutes.capitol.texas.gov.

title: Florida speeding fines double in a posted construction zone (s. 318.18(3)(e))
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: Florida doubles the speeding fine in a posted construction zone under section 318.18(3)(e), Florida Statutes. Two conditions: the zone is posted, with the posting stating the speed limit and that fines are doubled; and construction personnel are present or operating equipment on the road or immediately next to it. The regular fines in 318.18(3)(b) are $25 for 6 to 9 mph over, $100 for 10 to 14 over, $150 for 15 to 19 over, $175 for 20 to 29 over and $250 for 30 mph or more over, so doubled they are $50, $200, $300, $350 and $500, before court costs. No crew on or beside the road means no doubling, even with the signs up. FDOT work zone layouts are in the FDOT Standard Plans, Index 102 series, and FDOT requires its Temporary Traffic Control (MOT) training for people who set up and supervise work zones on state roads; those two points were not confirmed from an FDOT page here.

title: Washington flagger card rule (WAC 296-155-305)
topic: Traffic control: flaggers
text: Washington requires a flagger card by state safety rule. WAC 296-155-305(6): each flagger must have in their possession a valid Washington traffic control flagger card, or a valid card from a state that has a reciprocity agreement with Washington. The card shows the training completed, the date, the instructor, the issuing state and an expiration date no more than 3 years from issue, with a photo or the words valid with photo ID. Training is based on the MUTCD. The reciprocity states named are Oregon, Idaho and Montana, and the WSDOT standard specifications (1-10.3(1)A) likewise accept cards from those states. Someone without a card may flag only in an emergency, until a certified flagger takes over. Other points in the same rule: flaggers are used only when other traffic control is not enough; the employer orients each flagger to the site (the job, equipment, traffic pattern, signals with operators, an escape route on foot); a site-specific traffic control plan is kept on site for jobs longer than one day; flaggers may not be given other duties or use a cell phone or headphones while flagging; and they get a paid 10 minute rest for each 4 hours.
source: WAC 296-155-305(2), (6), (7), (9); WSDOT Standard Specifications 1-10.3(1)A

title: Washington flagging: sign sequence, flagger station distance, apparel and lighting
topic: Traffic control: flaggers
text: Washington's flagger rule, WAC 296-155-305, sets numbers the national manual leaves open. Advance warning signs: a three-sign sequence on roads posted below 45 mph and a four-sign sequence at 45 mph or higher. Flagger station distance ahead of the work space (Table 2): 20 mph 35 ft, 25 mph 55 ft, 30 mph 85 ft, 35 mph 120 ft, 40 mph 170 ft, 45 mph 220 ft, 50 mph 280 ft, 55 mph 335 ft, 60 mph 415 ft, 65 mph 485 ft; longer is acceptable. Flaggers stand on the shoulder next to the traffic they control or in the closed lane, and step into the lane only after traffic has stopped. Flaggers must not be exposed to traffic or equipment coming from behind unless there is a way to warn them, such as an observer or a mirror. Apparel in daylight: a Class 2 high-visibility garment and a high-visibility hard hat. In darkness, from half an hour before sunset to half an hour after sunrise: the Class 2 garment plus white coveralls or trousers with reflective leg bands, and a hard hat with at least 12 square inches of reflective material. Flagger stations are lit with floodlights at night, set so they do not glare at drivers. Sign spacing by road type is in the rule's Table 1; those values were not confirmed row by row here, so read the table.

title: Washington speeding in a roadway construction zone: double penalty (RCW 46.61.527)
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: Washington doubles the penalty for speeding in a roadway construction zone. RCW 46.61.527: a roadway construction zone is an area where public employees or private contractors are doing construction, repair or maintenance work on or next to a public road. A driver may not exceed the speed shown on the traffic control devices in the zone, and a speed infraction there carries twice the usual penalty, which may not be waived, reduced or suspended. The same section creates the crime of reckless endangerment of roadway workers, a gross misdemeanor: driving in a construction zone in a way that endangers or is likely to endanger people or property, or removing, evading or intentionally striking a traffic safety or control device. A conviction brings a 60 day license suspension. Standards for the devices on state highways are set by the Secretary of Transportation. The text read here showed amendments through 2009; later changes were not confirmed.

title: Oregon Temporary Traffic Control Handbook (OTTCH): the rules for jobs of 3 days or less
topic: Traffic control: which manual applies and flagger cards
text: Oregon's standard for short work zones is the Oregon Temporary Traffic Control Handbook, 2026 edition (January 2026), adopted through OAR 734-020-0005. It covers traffic control in place continuously for three days or less on any public road in the state. Longer jobs, or jobs more complicated than the handbook's diagrams, need a full traffic control plan. A traffic control plan is required whenever work is done on or along a public road; for short jobs the handbook diagram can be the plan. Flaggers: certified in Oregon, Washington, Idaho or Montana, at least 18 years old, retrained every three years, carrying the card (sections 3.2 and 3.3). When only flaggers are used, the distance between the Flagger signs should not be more than one mile; past that use a pilot car. Drivers should not be held longer than 20 minutes at a flagger station under normal conditions. Apparel: ANSI/ISEA 107-2015 or later, Type R, Class 2 or 3; flaggers Class 2 required and Class 3 recommended at night. Cone spacing: the posted speed in feet in a taper and twice that along the work. Cities and counties may be stricter and usually require a permit.
source: Oregon Temporary Traffic Control Handbook 2026 (ODOT), sections 1.1, 1.4, 2.3, 3.2, 3.3, 3.6, 3.8; OAR 734-020-0005

title: Oregon taper lengths and cone counts by speed (OTTCH Table 2-3)
topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
text: Oregon's Temporary Traffic Control Handbook 2026 prints taper lengths with the number of cones in Table 2-3. Merging taper for a 12 ft lane: 25 mph 125 ft (6 cones), 30 mph 180 ft (7), 35 mph 245 ft (8), 40 mph 320 ft (9), 45 mph 540 ft (13), 50 mph 600 ft (13), 55 mph 660 ft (13), 60 mph 720 ft (13), 65 mph 780 ft (13). For an 11 ft lane: 25 mph 115 ft, 30 mph 165 ft, 35 mph 225 ft, 40 mph 295 ft, 45 mph 495 ft, 55 mph 605 ft. For a 10 ft lane: 25 mph 105 ft, 30 mph 150 ft, 35 mph 205 ft, 40 mph 270 ft, 45 mph 450 ft, 55 mph 550 ft. Shifting tapers are half: 12 ft at 35 mph is 125 ft, at 45 mph 270 ft. Shoulder taper (10 ft shoulder): 25 mph 35 ft, 35 mph 70 ft, 45 mph 150 ft, 55 mph 185 ft. The formulas are the national ones (Tables 2-1 and 2-2). One-lane two-way and downstream tapers are 50 to 100 ft with 4 to 6 cones at 20 ft. Night flagger stations: lit separately from the work, light 15 to 21 ft high on the flagger's side, at least 5 foot-candles, flagger recognizable from 1,000 ft (sections 3.8, 4.3). Sign spacing and buffer lengths are in Table 2-4; those values were not confirmed here because the table did not read cleanly.
source: Oregon Temporary Traffic Control Handbook 2026, Tables 2-1, 2-2, 2-3; sections 2.3, 3.8, 4.3

title: Colorado work zone penalties and the signs that turn them on (C.R.S. 42-4-614)
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: Colorado increases penalties and surcharges for listed traffic violations inside a designated maintenance, repair or construction zone (C.R.S. 42-4-614, with the amounts in 42-4-1701(4)(c)). CDOT designates the zone on a state highway; on any other road the public entity doing the work does. A zone can be designated only when work is going on or will be within four hours. Signs make the zone: one sign before the work area telling drivers that increased penalties are in effect, and one after it telling them the increased penalties no longer apply. The zone runs from the first sign to the second. The signs must meet CDOT's requirements and may be on fixed, variable or movable stands, or on a moving vehicle for work such as striping. The size of the increase was not confirmed here; it is set in section 42-4-1701. Colorado flagger notes from CDOT: flaggers must speak and understand English, and fluorescent red apparel is not allowed for flaggers.
source: C.R.S. 42-4-614; C.R.S. 42-4-1701(4)(c); CDOT Flagger Program industry memo (Jan. 1, 2026)

title: Utah: obey the flagger, and double fines for speeding past workers (41-6a-209)
topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
text: Utah Code 41-6a-209 does two things. First, it is an offense to willfully fail or refuse to obey a lawful order or direction of a flagger at a highway construction or maintenance site who is using the devices and procedures required, the same as disobeying a peace officer or a school crossing guard. Second, for speeding in a highway construction or maintenance site, the court must set the fine at no less than double the amount in the uniform recommended fine schedule, but only if workers are present at the site and the site is clearly marked with signs warning drivers of the doubled fine. Without workers there, or without the signs, the doubling does not apply. Flaggers in the state must be trained and certified before flagging, and the certification lasts three years (UDOT Flagger Training and Certification page). The section's last listed amendment is from the 2005 General Session; later changes were not confirmed.
source: Utah Code 41-6a-209; UDOT Flagger Training & Certification page
